author: A Robot
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Establish the fundamental principle of VSEPR: electron domains around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. Introduce how to count electron domains from a Lewis structure.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand the electrostatic repulsion principle underlying VSEPR theory.
Learn how to count electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs) from a Lewis structure.
Recognize that VSEPR predicts 3D molecular geometry from a 2D Lewis structure.

components.text: Count domains: 2 bonds + 1 lone pair = 3 domains

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the central atom and displays a sample Lewis structure (water) with domain-counting rules. Establishes that VSEPR predicts 3D shape from 2D input.
clips.narration: Welcome to VSEPR theory. Electrons in bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel one another electrostatically. The molecule adopts whatever three-dimensional geometry places these electron domains as far apart as possible in space. We start with a Lewis structure — a flat, two-dimensional representation of where electrons are located. From the Lewis structure, we count electron domains: each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair counts as one domain.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasizes domain counting from the water Lewis structure, setting up the next scene's geometric rearrangement demonstration.
clips.narration: Here is a Lewis structure of water, H2O. The oxygen atom in the center has two O-H single bonds and two lone pairs of electrons. That gives us a steric number of 4: two bonding electron domains and two lone pair domains. Each of these four domains — bonding or lone — will repel the others and influence the final three-dimensional shape.

modules.description: Demonstrate how electron domains arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. Build up from 2 to 6 domains, showing linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral geometries. Display repulsion vectors and geometric parameters (angles) for each configuration.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Observe the minimum-repulsion principle in action as domains drift apart into optimal configurations.
Memorize the five electron-domain geometries and their characteristic angles (2→180°, 3→120°, 4→109.5°, 5→90°/120°, 6→90°).
Develop spatial reasoning by viewing geometries from multiple angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Two domains appear and slide into a linear configuration (180° apart). Repulsion vectors appear briefly and fade as the geometry stabilizes.
clips.narration: We begin with two electron domains around a central atom. Watch as they repel one another and drift apart. They settle 180 degrees apart — a linear arrangement. This is the linear electron-domain geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Third domain appears and all three drift into a trigonal planar arrangement. Geometry label updates and repulsion vectors appear momentarily.
clips.narration: Now we add a third electron domain. The three domains rearrange themselves, still repelling one another, and settle into a trigonal planar configuration at 120 degrees from one another in a plane.

clips.changeMeaning: Fourth domain appears, and all four drift into tetrahedral arrangement. Label updates, and geometry reference panel on the side becomes more prominent.
clips.narration: A fourth electron domain is added. The four domains now rearrange into a tetrahedral configuration, each pointing toward the corner of a tetrahedron. The angle between any two bonds is approximately 109.5 degrees. This is a very common geometry in chemistry.

clips.changeMeaning: Fifth and sixth domains appear and drift into their respective configurations. Geometry label cycles through both. Reference panel summarizes all five geometries clearly.
clips.narration: With five domains, the geometry becomes trigonal bipyramidal: three domains occupy the equatorial plane at 120 degrees from one another, while two domains occupy axial positions at 90 degrees to the equatorial plane. With a sixth domain, all six arrange themselves into an octahedral geometry, each at 90 degrees to its neighbors. You can rotate the molecule freely to see these geometries from any angle.

modules.description: Introduce the key distinction: electron-domain geometry describes how all domains (bonding and lone) arrange themselves; molecular geometry describes only the arrangement of atoms (bonding domains only). Show methane, ammonia, and water, demonstrating how the underlying electron-domain geometry (tetrahedral) remains constant while molecular geometry changes.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between electron-domain geometry (all domains) and molecular geometry (atoms only).
Understand that lone pairs occupy positions in the electron-domain geometry but are not part of the visible molecular shape.
Predict molecular geometry from electron-domain geometry and lone pair count.

clips.changeMeaning: Methane model appears. Label shows electron-domain and molecular geometries match.
clips.narration: Let's look at methane, CH4. The central carbon atom has four bonding domains — each C-H single bond is one domain. No lone pairs. So the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, and because all four domains are bonding pairs, the molecular geometry — the shape traced by the atoms — is also tetrahedral.

components.text:
Ammonia (NH3)
Electron-domain: Tetrahedral
Molecular: Trigonal Pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: Ammonia model appears. One of methane's bonding domains is replaced with a translucent lone-pair cloud. Label updates to show electron-domain (tetrahedral) vs. molecular (trigonal pyramidal).
clips.narration: Now consider ammonia, NH3. The central nitrogen has three bonding domains and one lone pair domain — a total of four electron domains. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral. But the lone pair is not 'seen' as an atom, so the molecular geometry — the shape of the atoms alone — is trigonal pyramidal: a triangular base with the nitrogen atom at the apex.

clips.changeMeaning: Water model appears. Two lone-pair clouds surround the oxygen. Label shows both geometries; electron-domain is still tetrahedral but molecular is now bent.
clips.narration: Finally, water, H2O. Oxygen has two bonding domains and two lone pair domains — four electron domains total. The electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral. But with two lone pairs removed from the visible shape, the molecular geometry is bent: the two hydrogen atoms and the oxygen form a bent structure.

modules.moduleName: Lone Pair Angular Asymmetry and Bond Angles
modules.description: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs. Lone pairs are attracted only to the central nucleus, so they spread out more; bonding pairs are shared between two nuclei and are more constrained. Display methane, ammonia, and water side-by-side with labeled bond angles, visually showing how H-X-H angles decrease (109.5° → 107° → 104.5°) as lone pairs are added.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand that lone pairs are held only by the central nucleus, making them more diffuse than bonding pairs.
Explain why bond angles deviate from idealized values in the presence of lone pairs.
Predict bond-angle trends from lone pair count.

components.text:
Lone pairs held only by central nucleus.
Bonding pairs shared between two nuclei.
Lone pairs occupy more angular space.

clips.changeMeaning: Methane, ammonia, and water displayed side-by-side with bond angles labeled. Lone-pair clouds rendered larger than bonding domains to show visually that they occupy more space.
clips.narration: Now let's look at how lone pairs affect bond angles. Here we have methane with four bonding domains and no lone pairs — the H-C-H bond angle is 109.5 degrees, the ideal tetrahedral angle. In ammonia, there are three bonding domains and one lone pair; the H-N-H bond angle is compressed to about 107 degrees. In water, there are two bonding domains and two lone pairs; the H-O-H bond angle is compressed further to 104.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Explanation text remains visible. Visual comparison emphasizes angle compression with additional molecular overlay.
clips.narration: Why does this happen? Lone pairs are attracted only to the central atom's nucleus. Bonding pairs, by contrast, are attracted to both the central nucleus and the nucleus of the bonded atom, making them more confined. Because lone pairs are more diffuse, they occupy more angular space and repel the bonding pairs more strongly, squeezing the bond angles smaller.

modules.description: Present a gallery of real molecules covering all five electron-domain geometries and multiple molecular geometries. Include CO2 (linear), BF3 (trigonal planar), CH4 (tetrahedral), PF5 (trigonal bipyramidal), SF6 (octahedral), NH3 (trigonal pyramidal), H2O (bent), and XeF4 (square planar). For each molecule, display the Lewis structure, the predicted geometry from VSEPR, and confirm that real structures match VSEPR predictions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR rules to a variety of real molecules.
Verify that experimentally observed structures match VSEPR predictions.
Recognize common molecular shapes and their geometric properties.

components.text:
CO2
Linear
2 bonding domains
0 lone pairs

clips.changeMeaning: CO2 and BF3 models appear with labels showing bonding domains, lone pair count, and predicted geometry. Labels confirm these match real experimental structures.
clips.narration: Let's walk through some real molecules. Carbon dioxide, CO2, has a central carbon with two double bonds to oxygen atoms and no lone pairs. The steric number is 2, so the electron-domain geometry is linear, and the molecular geometry is also linear: the molecule is a straight line with a 180-degree bond angle. Boron trifluoride, BF3, has three bonding domains and no lone pairs — trigonal planar with 120-degree angles.

clips.changeMeaning: CH4, PF5, and SF6 models appear and become highlighted. Labels show bonding counts and geometries. Demonstrates how VSEPR correctly predicts all three structures.
clips.narration: Methane, CH4, has four bonding domains and no lone pairs — tetrahedral. Phosphorus pentafluoride, PF5, has five bonding domains and no lone pairs — trigonal bipyramidal, with three equatorial bonds at 120 degrees and two axial bonds at 90 degrees to the equatorial plane. Sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, has six bonding domains — octahedral, with all bond angles at 90 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: NH3, H2O, and XeF4 models appear. Lone-pair positions are indicated. Labels show both electron-domain and molecular geometries, confirming VSEPR predictions again.
clips.narration: Now molecules with lone pairs. Ammonia, NH3, has three bonding domains and one lone pair — the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal. Water, H2O, has two bonding domains and two lone pairs — tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, but bent molecular geometry. Xenon tetrafluoride, XeF4, has four bonding domains and two lone pairs occupying the axial positions of the octahedral electron-domain geometry, producing a square planar molecular shape.

modules.description: Students apply VSEPR rules through interactive activities. First, they drag electron domains into the correct geometry based on domain count. Close with a comprehensive summary of all five electron-domain geometries, the electron-domain/molecular geometry distinction, lone pair effects, and application to real molecules.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR rules to predict geometries from steric number.
Distinguish electron-domain from molecular geometry in decision-making scenarios.
Synthesize all VSEPR concepts and verify predictions against observations.

components.text: Drag domains to form tetrahedral arrangement (109.5° angles).

VSEPR Summary

Electron-Domain Geometries:
2 domains: Linear (180°)
3 domains: Trigonal Planar (120°)
4 domains: Tetrahedral (109.5°)
5 domains: Trig. Bipyramidal
6 domains: Octahedral (90°)

Key Principles:
• Count bonding pairs + lone pairs
• Lone pairs occupy more space
• Electron-domain ≠ Molecular geometry
• VSEPR matches real structures

clips.changeMeaning: Draggable domains appear around the central atom. Challenge instruction appears. Domains begin in random positions; students must reposition them to match tetrahedral angles.
clips.narration: Now it's your turn. You see electron domains floating around a central atom. Your challenge is to drag them into the correct geometric arrangement. For a tetrahedral geometry, position the domains at the corners of a tetrahedron, with each domain about 109.5 degrees from its neighbors.

clips.changeMeaning: All challenge objects are hidden. Comprehensive summary panel displays, listing all five electron-domain geometries, key principles, and the distinction between electron-domain and molecular geometry. Audio reviews the entire learning arc.
clips.narration: Excellent work! Let's recap the five key ideas from this lab. First: the minimum-repulsion principle — electron domains arrange themselves to minimize mutual repulsion. Second: the five electron-domain geometries and their characteristic angles — linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral. Third: the distinction between electron-domain geometry, which includes all domains, and molecular geometry, which shows only atoms. Fourth: lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing bond angles to deviate from ideal values. And fifth: VSEPR predictions match experimentally observed molecular structures across a wide range of molecules. Use these principles to predict the shapes of molecules and understand why they adopt the geometries they do.
